summary: Brick tower lit in 1856 on a keeper's house west of Santa Barbara; the 1925 earthquake destroyed it, and a 24-foot steel tower in a closed Coast Guard compound replaced it.

structures.note: About 40 ft from the ground per the 1925 bulletin; the Archive gives 34 ft from base to lantern centre.
Story-and-a-half, outer wall stuccoed (Board, 1901). The Archive lists the dwelling as stone.
Built 1928 or 1935; the sources disagree (see events).

access.note: Inside a Coast Guard compound; grounds and tower closed to the public. Distant view only, from a lookout reached by continuing east on Meigs Road.

events.note: Brick tower built into a keeper's dwelling by George Nagle of San Francisco, paid $8,000
19 December 1856: fixed red light from a fourth-order Fresnel lens (LighthouseFriends gives the day; the Bulletin says established 1856)
Julia F. Williams takes the post after Albert J. Williams declines it
Lamp changed from a lard-oil to a mineral-oil lamp
Well about 50 feet deep dug to remedy the water supply; walled with brick
Galvanized iron windmill erected over the well, feeding a cistern
High-power flashing lens, formerly at Alcatraz Island, installed: fixed white changed to a white flash every 15 seconds
Earthquake of 29 June 1925 wrecked the brick tower, dwelling and oil house. The Archive's disposition says 1926.
Acting keeper found the house wrecked and rescued his mother, sister, brother and visiting relatives from it
Temporary acetylene light on a 35 ft frame tower, placed in commission 3 July 1925
Raymond H. Weeks acting keeper after his father Harley A. Weeks died in March 1925
LighthouseFriends: a more permanent tower was erected January 1928. The Archive dates the replacement beacon to 1935; sources disagree.
Revolving beacon used atop the enclosed steel tower from 1935 to 1977 (LighthouseFriends); the Archive gives 1935 as the replacement
Light temporarily discontinued 1 June to 11 July 1942
Coast Guard abolished the laborer/custodian/lamplighter position of Raymond H. Weeks in March 1948

tower, enclosed steel, 7.3 m (24 ft), standing (built 1928 or 1935)
corrections.why: The 7.3 m (24 ft) height belongs to the steel tower that replaced the brick tower. The 1856 brick tower stood about 40 ft from the ground and was wrecked by the earthquake of 29 June 1925 (Bulletin 1925, PDF pp. 25, 29).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: 1856 is the first light: the Board's 1901 report says the light 'was built in 1856', and the 1925 bulletin says the station 'was established' in 1856. The 1935 date belongs to the replacement beacon on the steel tower, not to the first light.
The brick tower of 1856 was destroyed on 29 June 1925 (Bulletin, PDF pp. 29, 43). OpenStreetMap maps the steel tower that replaced it; 'standing' applies to the steel tower only.

The Archive's record gives the dwelling as stone. The Board's 1901 report says the tower was 'of brick with the outer wall stuccoed', and the 1925 bulletin says 'story-and-a-half brick dwelling'. The Board and the bulletin are used.

LighthouseFriends gives Julia Williams's age as eighty-one when she fell in 1905. The birth date the Los Angeles Times printed in 1893 (12 July 1826) gives 78 or 79. The story states the LighthouseFriends figure and the birth date, and notes the mismatch.

notes_for_editor: (1) Tower height: the Bulletin (1925) gives the brick tower as about 40 ft from the ground (12.2 m, used); the Archive gives 34 ft to the lantern centre; the record's 7.3 m matches the steel tower. Unresolved. (2) Replacement date: LighthouseFriends gives January 1928 for a permanent tower and 1935-1977 for the beacon; the Archive's disposition gives 1935 and says the 1856 tower was destroyed in 1926, while the Bulletin says 29 June 1925. The story gives both LighthouseFriends dates and the 1937 bulletin. (3) The 1925 concrete-tower plan is a Lighthouse Service report not in the corpus, read only as LighthouseFriends quotes it. (4) Keeper tenure: the Archive has Albert J. Williams to 1860 and LighthouseFriends says four years (consistent). The Coast Guard historian's account (summarised on Wikipedia as nine years and a handover to his wife) could not be read: the archived copies show no text. Not used. (5) Julia Williams's birth and 1893 profile are from the Los Angeles Times as quoted by LighthouseFriends; the newspaper itself was not read. The 1897 Herald says thirty-five years; the 1865 appointment makes it about thirty-two. (6) After 1905 the Archive lists Caroline Morse (1905-1911). Wikipedia's lead names a Mrs. Jones as the woman who relieved Julia; not used. (7) Raymond H. Weeks: Archive principal keeper 1925-1948; LighthouseFriends calls him laborer/custodian/lamplighter to March 1948, and its own head-keeper list gives 1925-1943. The story uses the Archive span and LighthouseFriends' job description. (8) The Washington Daily News wire (30 June 1925) says Mrs. J. Weeks, widow of the former keeper, tended the light; the official account names the acting keeper as the son, so the wire is quoted as a disagreement only. A South Bend News-Times wire of 1 July 1925 gives 'Mrs. A. H. Weeks' as keeper of Point Conception, a different station; not used. (9) OCR: the 1920 Commissioner report (scan p. 578) reads 'built in 1866'; the 1921 and 1922 reports read 1856; 1856 is used. The 1920 OCR should be checked against the page image. (10) Candlepower: the Bulletin OCR reads '5S0.000' and LighthouseFriends gives 480,000 for the old light; not used. (11) Two Board descriptions disagree on direction: 'southeast of Santa Barbara Landing' (1894) and 'a few miles westerly of the city' (Bulletin 1925). Both are stated in the story. (12) No wreck tied to the light was found in the sources read; the 1925 earthquake is the only storm-type event. (13) 1893 and 1894 Board pages are OCR-damaged; the quotes use clean lines. (14) Current characteristic (Fl W 10s) and focal height in the record are not verified and are not used. (15) No photos added.
